text:
Open with the problem and the promise of the project: detect online card fraud, but keep the reasoning visible to an analyst. This presentation focuses on the method, the evidence, and what the Mauritius tests do and do not establish.
[Bullet points]
- Project goal: interpretable CNP fraud detection
- Mauritius-contextualised evaluation
- End-to-end path from data to analyst UI
[Sources]
- User-provided dissertation PDF, title page and abstract, pp. i-iv; User-provided dissertation PDF, Figure 4, p. 42; embedded crop used as the cover visual

name: aim-text
text: Build a CNP fraud detector that is accurate enough to be useful, explainable enough to review, and deployable enough to test in a Mauritius context.
textPreview: Build a CNP fraud detector that is accurate enough to be useful, explainable enough to review, and deployable enough to test in a Mauriti...

text:
The key framing is the imbalance. In this filtered dataset, fraud is only 1.21 percent of transactions, or roughly one fraud case for every 81 legitimate transactions. That is why I use precision, recall, F1 and PR-AUC as the main evidence rather than accuracy alone. The project also addresses interpretability and contextual validity.
[Bullet points]
- Fraud is only 1.21% of 294,854 transactions
- Accuracy can hide minority-class failures
- Precision, recall, F1 and PR-AUC are prioritised
[Sources]
- User-provided dissertation PDF, abstract p. iv and methodology pp. 27-29; User-provided dissertation PDF, problem statement pp. 4-6

name: feature-list
text: 7 named features: amount | hour | age | distance | amount z-score | category | gender
textPreview: 7 named features: amount | hour | age | distance | amount z-score | category | gender

text:
The data was filtered before feature engineering to keep the task specifically about card-not-present transactions. The seven features deliberately describe behaviour: transaction amount, time of day, age, distance from home, category-relative amount z-score, category and gender. The chronological split is intended to mimic training on historical transactions and predicting future ones.
[Bullet points]
- Filtered data: 294,854 CNP transactions and 3,576 fraud cases
- Named behavioural features keep the signal explainable
- Chronological 60/20/20 split mirrors future prediction
[Sources]
- User-provided dissertation PDF, methodology pp. 27-32, Tables 3-4; User-provided dissertation PDF, Figure 3, p. 31; embedded crop shown on slide; Project repository, backend/utils/feature_engineering.py and backend/datautils/preprocess.py

text:
The model comparison is intentionally compact: logistic regression provides an interpretable baseline, random forest captures non-linear rules, and XGBoost provides a stronger boosted detector. The final pipeline uses native class weighting rather than synthetic oversampling after SMOTE caused poor generalisation on new examples. Thresholds and the three-tier verdict are applied after model scoring.
[Bullet points]
- Logistic regression is the interpretable baseline
- Random Forest captures non-linear rules
- XGBoost provides a stronger boosted detector
[Sources]
- User-provided dissertation PDF, methodology pp. 33-38 and results pp. 57-60; Project repository, backend/models/train.py and backend/models/predict.py

name: accuracy-note
text: Accuracy is omitted from the chart because all three models exceed 99% under the 81:1 class imbalance.
textPreview: Accuracy is omitted from the chart because all three models exceed 99% under the 81:1 class imbalance.

text:
The important result is not the small difference in accuracy. XGBoost reaches 92.63 percent precision, 92.29 percent recall, 92.46 percent F1 and 97.60 percent PR-AUC. Random Forest is close, with identical recall and slightly lower precision. Logistic regression still detects most fraud, but at a much higher false-positive cost. PR-AUC is the most meaningful summary here because it focuses on the minority class.
[Bullet points]
- XGBoost is strongest standalone: 92.63% precision
- XGBoost reaches 92.29% recall and 97.60% PR-AUC
- Random Forest is close with 91.29% F1 and 96.23% PR-AUC
[Sources]
- User-provided dissertation PDF, Tables 10-11, pp. 58-59; User-provided dissertation PDF, discussion of RQ1, pp. 64-65

name: ensemble-note
text: 544/545 fraud cases were FRAUD BLOCKED; none were APPROVED. Block precision was 43.07% - the intentional cost of conservative escalation.
textPreview: 544/545 fraud cases were FRAUD BLOCKED; none were APPROVED. Block precision was 43.07% - the intentional cost of conservative escalation.

text:
This is the reliability story of the system. SHAP shows which features push a transaction toward fraud or legitimacy, and the natural-language explanation makes that understandable to a non-technical analyst. In the extreme E3 benchmark, logistic regression produced a 100 percent fraud probability while the two tree models did not. The escalation rule therefore takes the most severe model verdict. This improves sensitivity, but it creates a precision cost: many blocked transactions still require human review.
[Bullet points]
- SHAP identifies fraud and legitimacy drivers
- Natural-language explanations make the score reviewable
- The most-severe verdict rule protects against a missed signal
[Sources]

text:
The model is packaged as a usable workflow rather than left as an offline experiment. Analysts can submit single or batch predictions, see the ensemble verdict and SHAP explanation, inspect history and confirmed labels can be added as a future retraining loop. The three MUR benchmarks are deliberately illustrative. E1 and E3 behave as intended; E2 exposes a shift after CNP filtering, and the SHAP layer helps diagnose it.
[Bullet points]
- Analysts can run single, batch and historical predictions
- FastAPI connects the React UI to models and SQLite history
- E1 and E3 matched intent; E2 changed after CNP filtering

textPreview: Real Mauritian transaction data | Velocity and sequence features | Threshold calibration on held-out data

text:
Close with the balanced claim. The project contributes an interpretable feature pipeline, model comparison, SHAP explanations, an escalation rule and a working analyst-facing application. It does not yet establish statistical generalisation to Mauritius because the local test set contains only three manually constructed transactions. The clearest next steps are real local data, transaction velocity features and threshold calibration on a held-out partition. Then invite questions.
[Bullet points]
- Contributions: interpretable features, SHAP, escalation and a deployed app
- Main limitation: US-simulated data and three hand-made MUR benchmarks
- Next: local data, velocity features and held-out threshold calibration
[Sources]
- User-provided dissertation PDF, conclusion pp. 69-75; User-provided dissertation PDF, limitations and recommendations pp. 73-75

This is the concise conclusion. The model question is answered positively, the interpretability question is answered through SHAP and escalation, and the Mauritius question remains preliminary. Finish by stating exactly what the project demonstrates and what future data is required.
[Bullet points]
- RQ1: supervised learning detects fraud despite severe imbalance
- RQ2: SHAP and escalation make decisions more reviewable
- RQ3: Mauritius generalisation is promising but preliminary
